NIP-01 is the agreement that makes Nostr recognizable at all: events, signatures, filters, relay messages and the small grammar every later NIP depends on.
NIP-02 is the portable social graph: a kind 3 event that lets a user's follows move between clients instead of belonging to one app.
NIP-03 attaches Bitcoin-time proof to a Nostr event, but the current standards list marks it unrecommended because the design needs an update.
NIP-04 is the first Nostr encrypted-DM scheme: historically important, widely understood, and now officially legacy in favor of NIP-17.
NIP-05: Mapping Nostr keys to DNS-based internet identifiers
NIP-05 gives public keys a human-readable internet handle, but its own source is careful: this is identification, not ownership of the identity.
NIP-06: Basic key derivation from mnemonic seed phrase

NIP-06 is the historical bridge between Bitcoin-style seed phrases and Nostr keys, now marked unrecommended because normal users are safer with one well-kept nsec than a confused wallet-style account tree.
NIP-07: window.nostr capability for web browsers
NIP-07 made web Nostr clients practical by moving signing out of the website and into a browser signer, while still leaving every signing request as a product-trust decision.
NIP-08 is the old inline mention scheme for text notes, useful for reading legacy content but deprecated because NIP-27 gives references a cleaner and broader shape.
NIP-09 gives a user a signed way to ask relays to remove events, but it is deliberately a deletion request rather than a promise that history disappears everywhere.
NIP-10 is the grammar behind ordinary Nostr conversation: kind 1 notes, reply roots, direct parents, quote references and the notification context around them.
NIP-11 is the public label, policy sheet and capability document for a relay, giving clients a way to see what a relay claims before they treat it as infrastructure.
NIP-12 is the archived home of generic tag queries, the rule that made relay filters useful beyond authors and event IDs by letting clients ask for indexed tag values.
NIP-13 adds a small Bitcoin-flavored spam cost to Nostr events by mining event IDs with leading zero bits and committing the intended difficulty in a nonce tag.
NIP-14: Subject tag in text events
NIP-14 is a small subject-line standard for kind 1 text events, useful where a Nostr conversation wants the scanability of email-style threads.

NIP-15 tried to make resilient commerce portable on Nostr with stalls, products, checkout messages and auctions, but the official source now warns that the design is too complicated and points people toward NIP-99.
NIP-16 is the archived source of Nostr's event-lifetime idea: regular, replaceable, ephemeral and addressable behavior, now folded into NIP-01 where every relay has to learn it.
NIP-17 is the modern Nostr DM scheme: kind 14 message rumors sealed with NIP-44 and gift-wrapped through NIP-59 so public relays move private chat with less metadata leakage.
NIP-18 defines how Nostr content travels through other people's feeds: simple reposts for kind 1 notes, q-tag quote references and generic reposts for non-note events.
NIP-19 gives Nostr its copy-paste language: npub, nsec, note, nprofile, nevent and naddr strings that humans can recognize while clients still store hex and binary internally.
NIP-20 is the origin of relay command results: the OK and CLOSED feedback language that tells clients whether an event was accepted, rejected, duplicated, rate-limited or blocked.
NIP-21 wraps NIP-19 identifiers in nostr: links so websites, apps and operating systems can hand profiles, events and addressable objects to a user's Nostr client.
NIP-22 is the structured comment layer for Nostr objects beyond ordinary notes, using kind 1111 with uppercase root tags and lowercase parent tags.
NIP-23 is Nostr's article format: addressable kind 30023 events with Markdown content, metadata tags, naddr links and NIP-22 comments.
NIP-24: Extra metadata fields and tags
NIP-24 is Nostr's small registry for de facto metadata: display names, websites, banners, bot flags, birthdays, shared tags and deprecated fields that clients already meet in the wild.
NIP-25 defines Nostr reactions: kind 7 events for likes, dislikes and emoji responses, plus kind 17 reactions for external content such as websites and podcast episodes.
NIP-26 tried to let one key sign events on behalf of another, but it is now marked unrecommended because the security, relay and UX burden outweighed the gain.
NIP-27 defines how readable Nostr content embeds profile, event and address references inline through nostr: links, while tags handle notifications and indexing separately.
NIP-28 is the older public-channel chat model for Nostr, now marked unrecommended because the ecosystem moved toward NIP-29 relay-based groups for serious community rooms.
NIP-29 defines Nostr groups whose membership, moderation and metadata are enforced by relays, with group IDs, h tags, role events, join requests and optional LiveKit AV rooms.
NIP-30 defines custom emoji tags for Nostr profiles, notes, reactions and user statuses, mapping :shortcode: text to image URLs and optional emoji-set addresses.
NIP-31 is the alt-tag fallback for custom event kinds, now marked unrecommended but still useful for understanding how unknown Nostr objects can remain minimally readable.
NIP-32 defines Nostr labels: namespaced L and l tags plus kind 1985 label events for distributed moderation, classification, licensing and collection management.
NIP-33 is the old home of addressable events, the mechanism that lets Nostr objects such as articles, lists and app records keep stable coordinates while newer versions replace older ones.

NIP-34 tries to move Git collaboration into Nostr: repository announcements, clone hints, issues, patches, pull requests, status events and review comments without making one forge the permanent center.
NIP-35 makes Nostr a searchable announcement layer for BitTorrent metadata: enough tags to find a torrent and build a magnet link, without pretending Nostr relays host the files.
NIP-36 defines the content-warning tag: a small author-side warning that lets clients hide sensitive events until you chooses to open them.
NIP-37 gives Nostr clients a private draft format: encrypted unsigned events, checkpoints and private storage relay hints for work that is not ready to publish.
NIP-38 is the lightweight live-status standard: addressable kind 30315 events for what someone is doing, listening to or temporarily pointing people toward.
NIP-39: Linking Profiles to Other Platforms
NIP-39 lets a user attach proof-backed external identities to their Nostr key through kind 10011 and i tags, moving the claim out of profile metadata and into its own event.
NIP-40 defines the expiration tag: a timestamp that tells relays and clients when an event needs to be treated as expired, while warning people not to confuse expiry with secrecy.
NIP-42: Authentication of clients to relays

NIP-42 gives relays a signed challenge-response login for specific jobs: publishing, reading restricted data, paid access, private relay use and any policy where the relay needs to know which pubkey is behind the current connection.
NIP-43: Relay Access Metadata and Requests
NIP-43 adds a small membership and invite layer around relays: who appears to have access, how add and remove events are announced, and how a user can request admission with a claim string.

NIP-44 is the encryption workhorse behind modern private Nostr flows: a versioned payload format using secp256k1 ECDH, HKDF, padding, ChaCha20 and HMAC, with clear warnings about what it still cannot protect.
NIP-45 adds COUNT to the relay protocol so clients can ask how many events match a filter without downloading every matching event just to count them.
NIP-46 lets a client use a Nostr identity without holding the user's private key: requests go to a remote signer, often called a bunker, which approves and signs on the user's behalf.

NIP-47 is the bridge between Nostr apps and Lightning wallets: clients send encrypted wallet requests over relays, wallet services answer, and users can connect payment capability without handing every app direct wallet control.
NIP-48 defines the proxy tag so Nostr events imported from ActivityPub, AT Protocol, RSS or the open web can point back to their original object instead of pretending they were born on Nostr.
NIP-49 defines ncryptsec, an encrypted export format for a Nostr private key using password-based scrypt derivation and XChaCha20-Poly1305.
NIP-50 adds a search field to relay filters so clients can ask relays for human-language matches instead of only exact ids, authors, kinds and tags.
NIP-51 is the user's portable shelf system for Nostr: follows, mutes, bookmarks, relay choices, communities, badge displays, curation sets and private lists that can move between clients.
NIP-52 gives Nostr addressable calendar objects: date events, time events, calendars, RSVP events and collaborative requests so events can travel without belonging to one platform calendar.
NIP-53 describes live activities on Nostr: streaming rooms, speaker lists, participant roles, live chat, status changes, recordings and proof that named guests agreed to participate.
NIP-54 defines Nostr wiki articles as addressable events, with normalized subjects, Djot content, wikilinks, merge requests and multiple competing articles about the same topic.
NIP-55 lets Android clients ask a local signer app to return a pubkey, sign events and encrypt or decrypt payloads without the client handling the user's private key.
NIP-56 defines kind 1984 reports so users, clients and relays can signal spam, malware, impersonation, illegal content or other objectionable material without creating a central moderation authority.
NIP-57 is the standard that made public Lightning payments native to Nostr: zap requests, zap receipts, LNURL support, relays, comments and verification rules.
NIP-58 defines badge definitions, badge awards, profile badge displays and badge sets so recognition can move with a user's Nostr identity.
NIP-59 wraps an event in layers called rumor, seal and gift wrap, using NIP-44 encryption to hide more metadata for private messages and other encapsulated events.
NIP-5A turns a Nostr key into a static website publisher: signed site manifests map URL paths to Blossom content hashes, while named sites, snapshots and aggregate hashes make the site portable.
NIP-60 stores Cashu wallet state on Nostr relays: encrypted wallet configuration, encrypted unspent proofs and optional encrypted spending history that can follow the user across apps.
NIP-61 is the Cashu-native cousin of Lightning zaps: a sender publishes a P2PK-locked Cashu token to the recipient, and the payment itself becomes the receipt.
NIP-62 gives a Nostr key a signed way to ask relays to delete everything tied to that pubkey, including old deletion requests and relevant gift wraps, up to the request timestamp.
NIP-64 gives chess games a simple Nostr event kind: kind 64 notes contain PGN so clients can render a board, validate legal moves and preserve a game in a format chess software already understands.
NIP-65 is the outbox/inbox map for Nostr: a user publishes kind 10002 to say where they write events and where they read mentions, so other clients know which relays to use.
NIP-66: Relay Discovery and Liveness Monitoring
NIP-66 turns relay observation into signed Nostr data: monitors publish discovery events about relay health, capabilities, network type, requirements and measurement checks.
NIP-67 adds optional finish and more hints to EOSE so clients can know whether a relay sent all stored events for a subscription or whether pagination needs to continue.

NIP-68 gives image-first Nostr clients their own event kind: kind 20 posts carry title, description and complete image metadata through imeta tags rather than hiding the picture inside a normal text note.
NIP-69 standardizes peer-to-peer trade order events so separate P2P Bitcoin marketplaces can publish buy and sell offers into a shared Nostr liquidity pool.

NIP-70 defines the protected-event tag, a simple '-' marker that tells relays an event is meant to be published by its authenticated author and is not meant to be blindly republished by third parties.
NIP-71 gives video-centric clients dedicated event kinds for normal, short and addressable videos, with imeta variants, duration, bitrate, thumbnails, fallbacks and audio-track metadata.
NIP-72 defines Reddit-style public communities with community definitions, moderator approvals and scoped comments, but it is now marked unrecommended in favor of NIP-29 for new group work.
NIP-73 standardizes i and k tags for global identifiers such as URLs, ISBNs, podcast GUIDs, ISANs, DOIs, geohashes, countries and blockchain transactions.
NIP-75 defines kind 9041 fundraising goals that can be zapped, tallied from listed relays and linked from profiles, long-form posts, badges, live streams or other addressable events.
NIP-77 wraps the Negentropy set-reconciliation protocol for Nostr so clients and relays can compare event sets with less bandwidth than sending every event or every ID.
NIP-78 gives apps a remoteStorage-like place for custom user data on Nostr relays: addressable kind 30078 and normal kind 78 for app-specific state that does not aim for broad interoperability.
NIP-7D defines simple forum threads: a kind 11 root thread with a title, and NIP-22 kind 1111 comments as replies, avoiding deep arbitrary reply trees.

NIP-84 turns highlighting into a portable Nostr object: kind 9802 records a selected passage, its source, attribution, context and optional quote commentary without reducing the act of reading to another short note.

NIP-85 lets Nostr clients consume signed rankings, counts and web-of-trust calculations from chosen providers, while making the trust tradeoff explicit instead of pretending every client can compute the whole network locally.

NIP-86 gives relay operators an HTTP JSON-RPC-like management surface for bans, allowlists, moderation queues, relay metadata, event-kind policy and admin access without turning those controls into client feed behavior.
NIP-87 lets Cashu and Fedimint mints announce themselves on Nostr and lets users publish signed recommendations, turning ecash mint discovery into a social trust question instead of a hardcoded list.

NIP-88 defines poll questions and response events for Nostr, including single-choice and multiple-choice behavior, relay hints and counting rules, while leaving the hard parts of identity and manipulation visible.
NIP-89 lets Nostr apps advertise which event kinds they can open and lets users recommend handlers, so an unknown event can lead to the right web, mobile or native client instead of a dead end.

NIP-90 describes a Nostr-native market for on-demand computation, where customers publish job requests, service providers return results and payment can be negotiated, but the standard is now marked unrecommended because the generic model grew too broad.

NIP-92 gives media URLs inside Nostr events an inline metadata tag, imeta, so clients can render images, videos and files with hashes, dimensions, alt text, blurhashes and fallbacks instead of guessing from a bare link.

NIP-94 defines kind 1063 file metadata events for shared files, giving Nostr a way to describe URLs, hashes, MIME types, sizes, thumbnails, alt text and fallbacks without pretending social notes are file storage.
NIP-96 defines a REST-style upload and management API for Nostr-aware HTTP file servers, but it is now marked unrecommended and deprecated in favor of Blossom/NIP-B7 for new media storage work.
NIP-98 lets a Nostr key authorize an HTTP request by signing a short-lived kind 27235 event that binds the request URL, method and optional payload hash to the user's public key.
NIP-99 defines addressable classified-listing events for products, services, rentals, gigs and offers, giving Nostr a flexible marketplace primitive without adopting the heavier structure of NIP-15.
NIP-A0 gives short voice notes their own Nostr event kinds, with direct audio URLs, reply structure through NIP-22 and optional waveform and duration metadata through imeta.
NIP-A4 defines kind 24 as a plaintext public message addressed to one or more users, meant for notification-style replies rather than feeds, private DMs or persistent chat threads.
NIP-B0 defines editable web bookmarks as kind 39701 events, making saved URLs portable, taggable, commentable and queryable by a normalized d tag instead of trapped inside one bookmarking app.

NIP-B7 explains how Nostr clients need to use Blossom media servers and kind 10063 server lists to recover, verify and route content-addressed blobs by SHA-256 instead of relying on one fragile media URL.

NIP-BE sketches a Bluetooth Low Energy transport for Nostr-style messages, but it is marked unrecommended because it appears to have been implemented once and needs serious review before builders rely on it.

NIP-C0 defines kind 1337 for code snippets, adding language, filename, extension, runtime, license, dependency and repository metadata so shared code can be rendered and discovered as code instead of plain notes.
NIP-C7 defines kind 9 chat messages as a lightweight ordered chat stream, separate from NIP-28 public chat channels and from encrypted DMs, with replies represented by quoted parent messages.

NIP-CC brings geocaching to Nostr with addressable cache listings, found logs, comment logs, geohash discovery, difficulty and terrain metadata, verification keys and optional mission-style claim rules.
NIP-EE: E2EE Messaging using MLS Protocol

NIP-EE adapted Messaging Layer Security to Nostr for private group messaging with forward secrecy and post-compromise security, but it is now marked unrecommended because the Marmot Protocol supersedes it.

NIP-F4 proposes Nostr-native podcast metadata and episode events so podcast clients can fetch shows from relays, link individual episodes, discover authors and connect comments, zaps and listening activity without depending only on RSS.
